title: Given two strings, return the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions, or replacements needed to turn the first string into the second.
shortTitle: Edit Distance — minimum insert, delete, replace (Levenshtein)

s1_definition.profdef: 2D DP (Levenshtein) where dp[i][j] is the edit distance between the first i characters of A and first j of B. If characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]; otherwise dp[i][j] = 1 + min(delete dp[i−1][j], insert dp[i][j−1], replace dp[i−1][j−1]). Borders are dp[i][0]=i and dp[0][j]=j. Time and space O(m·n).
s1_definition.analogy: The data-quality team at National Bank of India must fix a mistyped account holder name into the official spelling using the fewest single-letter edits. If the current letters agree, no edit is needed there; if they differ, pick the cheapest of deleting, inserting, or replacing.
s1_definition.oneliner: Match ⇒ diagonal; mismatch ⇒ 1 + min(delete, insert, replace).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** 2D DP (Levenshtein) where dp[i][j] is the edit distance between the first i characters of A and first j of B. If characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]; otherwise dp[i][j] = 1 + min(delete dp[i−1][j], insert dp[i][j−1], replace dp[i−1][j−1]). Borders are dp[i][0]=i and dp[0][j]=j. Time and space O(m·n).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The data-quality team at National Bank of India must fix a mistyped account holder name into the official spelling using the fewest single-letter edits. If the current letters agree, no edit is needed there; if they differ, pick the cheapest of deleting, inserting, or replacing.

**One line to remember:** Match ⇒ diagonal; mismatch ⇒ 1 + min(delete, insert, replace).

sections.s2_technical:
Build a table of size (m+1) by (n+1). The first column dp[i][0] is i because turning an i-length prefix into an empty string needs i deletions, and the first row dp[0][j] is j because building a j-length string from empty needs j insertions. These borders are the base cases.

When A.charAt(i−1) equals B.charAt(j−1) no operation is needed, so dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]. For example: `if (a.charAt(i-1)==b.charAt(j-1)) dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1];`. Otherwise take one plus the cheapest neighbor: delete from A is dp[i−1][j], insert into A is dp[i][j−1], and replace is dp[i−1][j−1]: `else dp[i][j]=1+Math.min(dp[i-1][j-1], Math.min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]));`.

The answer is dp[m][n], time and space O(m·n), reducible to two rows. A senior nuance is that edit distance powers spell-checkers and fuzzy name matching in KYC, and weighting the three operations differently produces generalized variants.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, KYC records sometimes contain a mistyped holder name, and the team must know how far it is from the official spelling to flag likely typos versus genuinely different people. This is exactly how Edit Distance works.

Problem 2 — A plain equality check only says same or different, not how close, which cannot drive a fuzzy-match threshold. This is exactly why the minimum-operations DP is used.

The mini-project builds a `NameMatcher`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input strings are horse and ros.

Step 1: The borders are filled, so dp of i and zero is i and dp of zero and j is j, representing pure deletions or insertions.

Step 2: Comparing h to r is a mismatch, taking one plus the cheapest neighbor.

Step 3: The run toward turning horse into ros accumulates a replace of h with r, a delete of a letter, and a replace of e with s.

Step 4: Matching letters like o and o copy the diagonal with no added cost.

Step 5: The bottom-right cell holds three, and Rajesh to Rajes needs a single deletion so it holds one.

```text
2026-10-27T01:50:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — KYC Name Matcher (Edit Distance)
2026-10-27T01:50:00Z [INFO] editDistance(Rajesh,Rajes) = 1
2026-10-27T01:50:00Z [INFO] Rajesh vs Rajes → 1
2026-10-27T01:50:00Z [INFO] editDistance(horse,ros) = 3
2026-10-27T01:50:00Z [INFO] horse vs ros → 3
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Edit Distance, also called Levenshtein distance, is a two-dimensional dynamic programming problem. I define dp of i and j as the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions, or replacements to turn the first i characters of one string into the first j characters of the other. The borders are the base cases: turning a prefix into empty costs one deletion per character, and building a prefix from empty costs one insertion per character.

For the body, when the current characters match I copy the diagonal cell because no edit is needed there. When they differ I take one plus the cheapest of three neighbors: the cell above is a deletion, the cell to the left is an insertion, and the diagonal is a replacement. The answer is the bottom-right cell, and I can shrink the space to two rows because each row only needs the one before it.

In my project at National Bank of India, KYC records sometimes had a mistyped holder name, and we needed to know how far it was from the official spelling to tell a likely typo from a genuinely different person. A plain equality check only says same or different, so I used this minimum-operations DP to drive a fuzzy-match threshold, which is the same idea behind spell-checkers.
